{{Short description|Point on a nonsingular algebraic curve}}
In [[mathematics]], a '''Weierstrass point''' <math>P</math> on a nonsingular [[algebraic curve]] <math>C</math> defined over the complex numbers is a point such that there are more functions on <math>C</math>, with their [[pole (complex analysis)|pole]]s restricted to <math>P</math> only, than would be predicted by the [[Riemann–Roch theorem]]. 

The concept is named after [[Karl Weierstrass]].

Consider the [[vector space]]s

:<math>L(0), L(P), L(2P), L(3P), \dots</math>

where <math>L(kP)</math> is the space of [[meromorphic function]]s on <math>C</math> whose order at <math>P</math> is at least <math>-k</math> and with no other poles.  We know three things: the dimension is at least 1, because of the constant functions on <math>C</math>; it is non-decreasing; and from the Riemann–Roch theorem the dimension eventually increments by exactly 1 as we move to the right. In fact if <math>g</math> is the [[genus (mathematics)|genus]] of <math>C</math>, the dimension from the <math>k</math>-th term is known to be

:<math>l(kP) = k - g + 1,</math> for <math>k \geq 2g - 1.</math>

Our knowledge of the sequence is therefore

:<math>1, ?, ?, \dots, ?, g, g + 1, g + 2, \dots.</math>

What we know about the ? entries is that they can increment by at most 1 each time (this is a simple argument: <math>L(nP)/L((n-1)P)</math> has dimension as most 1 because if <math>f</math> and <math>g</math> have the same order of pole at <math>P</math>, then <math>f+cg</math> will have a pole of lower order if the constant <math>c</math> is chosen to cancel the leading term). There are <math>2g - 2</math> question marks here, so the cases <math>g = 0</math> or <math>1</math> need no further discussion and do not give rise to Weierstrass points.

Assume therefore <math>g \geq 2</math>. There will be <math>g - 1</math> steps up, and <math>g</math> steps where there is no increment. A '''non-Weierstrass point''' of <math>C</math> occurs whenever the increments are all as far to the right as possible: i.e. the sequence looks like

:<math>1, 1, \dots, 1, 2, 3, 4, \dots, g - 1, g, g + 1, \dots.</math>

Any other case is a '''Weierstrass point'''. A '''Weierstrass gap''' for <math>P</math> is a value of <math>k</math> such that no function on <math>C</math> has exactly a <math>k</math>-fold pole at <math>P</math> only. The gap sequence is

:<math>1, 2, \dots, g</math>

for a non-Weierstrass point. For a Weierstrass point it contains at least one higher number. (The '''Weierstrass gap theorem''' or '''Lückensatz''' is the statement that there must be <math>g</math> gaps.)

For [[hyperelliptic curve]]s, for example, we may have a function <math>F</math> with a double pole at <math>P</math> only. Its powers have poles of order <math>4, 6</math> and so on. Therefore, such a <math>P</math> has the gap sequence

:<math>1, 3, 5, \dots, 2g - 1.</math>

In general if the gap sequence is

:<math>a, b, c, \dots</math>

the '''weight''' of the Weierstrass point is

:<math>(a - 1) + (b - 2) + (c - 3) + \dots.</math>

This is introduced because of a counting theorem: on a [[Riemann surface]] the sum of the weights of the Weierstrass points is <math>g(g^2 - 1).</math>

For example, a hyperelliptic Weierstrass point, as above, has weight <math>g(g - 1)/2.</math> Therefore, there are (at most) <math>2(g + 1)</math> of them.
The <math>2g+2</math> ramification points of the [[ramified covering]] of degree two from a hyperelliptic curve to the [[projective line]] are all hyperelliptic Weierstrass points and these exhausts all the Weierstrass points on a hyperelliptic curve of genus <math>g</math>.

Further information on the gaps comes from applying [[Clifford's theorem on special divisors|Clifford's theorem]]. Multiplication of functions gives the non-gaps a [[numerical semigroup]] structure, and an old question of [[Adolf Hurwitz]] asked for a characterization of the semigroups occurring. A new necessary condition was found by R.-O. Buchweitz in 1980 and he gave an example of a [[subsemigroup]] of the nonnegative integers with 16 gaps that does not occur as the semigroup of non-gaps at a point on a curve of genus 16 (see <ref>{{harvnb|Eisenbud|Harris|1987|loc=page 499.}}</ref>). A definition of Weierstrass point for a nonsingular curve over a [[field (mathematics)|field]] of positive [[characteristic (field)|characteristic]] was given by F. K. Schmidt in 1939.

== Positive characteristic ==
More generally, for a nonsingular [[algebraic curve]] <math>C</math> defined over an algebraically closed field <math>k</math> of characteristic <math>p \geq 0</math>, the gap numbers for all but finitely many points is a fixed sequence <math>\epsilon_1, ..., \epsilon_g.</math> These points are called '''non-Weierstrass points'''.
All points of <math>C</math> whose gap sequence is different are called '''Weierstrass''' points.

If <math>\epsilon_1, ..., \epsilon_g = 1, ..., g</math> then the curve is called a '''classical curve'''.
Otherwise, it is called '''non-classical'''. In characteristic zero, all curves are classical.

Hermitian curves are an example of non-classical curves. These are projective curves defined over finite field <math>GF(q^2)</math> by equation <math>y^q + y = x^{q+1}</math>, where <math>q</math> is a prime power.
